labelChirho: stand by, stand near, appear to
descriptionChirho: To stand by or near someone, to take a position beside a person; the intransitive aorist/perfect sense of physically positioning oneself in proximity, often with connotations of appearing or presenting oneself. Used of an angel standing by the shepherds (Luke 2:9), Jesus standing over Simon's mother-in-law to heal her fever (Luke 4:39), the chief priests and scribes standing against Jesus (Luke 20:1), two men in gleaming clothes standing by the women at the tomb (Luke 24:4), the men sent by Cornelius standing at the gate (Acts 10:17; 11:11), an angel standing by Peter in prison (Acts 12:7), Ananias standing near Paul (Acts 22:13), Paul standing by at Stephen's martyrdom (Acts 22:20), and the Lord standing by Paul in the night (Acts 23:11). Multilingual glosses center on physical standing/presence: arb: وقف (stood), deu: steht dabei (stands by), heb: עמד (stood), hin: खड़ा होना (stand), kor: 나타나다/서다 (appear/stand), spa: presentarse (present oneself).

To come upon someone suddenly or unexpectedly, to appear without warning; emphasizes the surprise or abruptness of arrival rather than mere spatial proximity. Used of Anna the prophetess coming up at the very moment Simeon was speaking in the temple (Luke 2:38), Martha's sister Mary approaching Jesus while he was teaching (Luke 10:40), the warning that 'that day' will come upon you suddenly like a snare (Luke 21:34), the priests and Sadducees coming upon the apostles while they were teaching (Acts 4:1), false witnesses coming upon Stephen (Acts 6:12), Claudius Lysias coming upon the mob beating Paul (Acts 23:27), and sudden destruction coming upon the ungodly like a thief in the night (1 Thess 5:3). Multilingual glosses reflect suddenness: arb: جاء/هجموا (came/attacked), eng: came upon/having come upon, heb: עמדו על/התנפלו (stood upon/fell upon), hin: आकर (having come), kor: 다가왔다/갑자기 다가와서 (approached/suddenly approached), spa: vinieron sobre/presentandose (came upon/presenting).

labelChirho: be present, be at hand, be imminent
descriptionChirho: To be present, to have arrived, to be at hand or imminent; the perfect/resultative sense describing a state of having come and now being present, often of abstract or temporal realities. Used of the coming winter that was now at hand and threatening the sea voyage (Acts 28:2) and of the time of Paul's departure having come (2 Tim 4:6). Multilingual glosses reflect imminence and arrival: arb: حاضر/حضر (present/arrived), eng: having set in / has come, heb: עומד/הגיעה (standing/has arrived), hin: आई हुई/आ पहुँच (having come/has arrived), kor: 닥친/다가왔다 (impending/has come), spa: que estaba sobre/ha llegado (that was upon/has arrived). This stative/resultative sense is distinct from the punctiliar 'come upon suddenly' in describing an ongoing condition rather than an abrupt event.

labelChirho: be ready, be urgent, press on
descriptionChirho: To be persistent, urgent, or ready; an imperatival use urging readiness and diligence in ministry. Used in 2 Tim 4:2 where Paul exhorts Timothy to 'preach the word; be ready in season and out of season' — a call to constant alertness and preparedness for ministry opportunities. Multilingual glosses diverge instructively: arb: اثبت (be firm/stand fast), deu: (untranslated), eng: be ready, heb: התיצב (station yourself/take your stand), hin: तैयार रह (stay ready), kor: 힘써라 (strive/be diligent), spa: insiste (insist/persist). The semantic range across languages — firmness, readiness, self-positioning, striving, insistence — captures the urgency and persistence implied by this imperative. This metaphorical extension from physical standing to spiritual readiness is a distinct sense from the literal spatial meanings.

To come upon someone with hostile intent, to attack or rush upon aggressively; used in Acts 17:5 where jealous Jews, having gathered a mob, attacked the house of Jason seeking to bring Paul and Silas before the people. Multilingual glosses clearly indicate hostility: arb: هاجموا (they attacked), eng: having attacked, heb: עומדים על (standing against), hin: आकर (having come), kor: 습격하여 (having raided/assaulted), spa: presentandose ante (presenting themselves before). This hostile sense is related to but distinct from the neutral 'come upon suddenly' sense — here the coming upon is specifically aggressive and violent rather than merely surprising.
